description.narrative: Sida's bidrag till FN:s fredsfond för Colombia. Fonden ger bidrag till insatser för stabilisering förtroendeskapande samt genomförandet av fredsavtalet mellan den colombianska regeringen och FARC, i syfte att: 1. Öka lokalbefolkningens förtroende för statliga institutioner på nationell och lokal nivå. 2. Öka människors och i synnerhet offren och / medborgares förtroende för fredsprocessen i de områden som drabbats hårdast av konflikten. 3. Förhindra och/eller minska brott och våld i samband med utbrott av väpnade konflikter och demobiliseringsprocesser. 4. Hantera konfliktsituationer på lokal nivå genom tidiga insatser (rapid response). 5. Bidra till att skapa fredsvinster, konkreta positiva förbättringar för människors dagliga liv, inom områdena säkerhet, rättvisa och utveckling. Andra givare till fonden inkluderar Canada, Irland, Norge, Storbritannien, Tyskland, och Schweiz.

The support to the UN multi-partner Trust Fund for Colombia ("contribution to specific-purpose programmes and funds") promotes actions for stabilisation, building trust, and the implementation of the Peace Agreement between the Colombian government and FARC. The Fund intends to address the root causes of the conflict, particularly in remote rural areas of the country. The Fund works within four thematic areas: 1) Stabilization; 2) Reincorporation; 3) Victim's rights and transitional justice; 4) Communication.

The overall objective of UN Multi Partner Trust Fund is to support the construction of peace in Colombia, contributing to the implementation of the Peace Agreement agreed between the Colombian Government and the former FARC-EP in 2016, as well as other actions related to peace building established by the National Government.
The fund's theory of change considers the context and address the root causes of the conflict, particularly in remote rural areas of the country with a historical weak institutional presence and capacity. A third phase of the fund was approved by the Steering Committee in June 2023.
The theory of change of the third phase consists of five thematic areas, each with its own objectives:
1) Sustainable human development: to promote comprehensive rural reform, rural development and human security with the objective of closing historical gaps, reducing inequality and strengthening security.
Under this area, a sub-area is included that seeks to support the national Government in the implementation of the Comprehensive Action against Antipersonnel Mines (AICMA).
2) Reincorporation: to strengthen the reintegration route of the ex-combatants, under a sustainability approach and in this way promote their effective inclusion in social dynamics, political and economic aspects of civil life, encouraging coexistence, reconciliation and not stigmatization.
3) Victim's rights and transitional justice: to support initiatives in line with the system set up in the peace agreement on Justice, Truth, Reparation and no Repetition.
4) Communication: to constant follow-up of the fund with a permanent, efficient and transparent communication.
5) Peace building beyond the 2016 Agreement: to support on-going and possible future peace negotiations as well as support initiatives to reduce violence, promote peace building, trust, and participation of communities and civil society.
The specific objectives for each of these areas are explained in greater detail in the Terms of Reference and Manual of operations of the fund.

description.narrative:
To the latest information (10.12.2025) the fund has received a total of USD 258,8M in contributions including interests, USD 226,7M have been allocated. Swedish contributions to the Fund amount USD 23.1M. The current phase of the Fund (Phase 3) had approved 58 projects and 5 call for proposals, the 36% of the resources has been allocated to gender. Since it´s creation, the Fund has approved a total of 344 projects reaching approximately 2.2 million people in 620 municipalities. 62% of the projects approved during phase 3 have been implemented by Civil Society Organizations.
The annual report for 2024 highlights some results achieved by the fund:
- Human development: One initiative resulted in a minimum viable model for land acquisition that addresses legal, socio ecosystemic and institutional risks associated with purchasing and allocating land including gender sensitive protocols, digital cartography tools and legal frameworks. UNMPTF supported the design of land purchasing risk analysis tool in partnership with Universidad de los Andes and national agencies and the fund also contributed to the start-up of Colombia's new Agrarian and Rural Jurisdiction (JAR) through three key areas: raising awareness and building knowledge about the jurisdiction among judges and rural communities; strengthening institutional coordination between local and national entities to support case management; and delivering a set of policy recommendations to the Ministry of Justice to guide the launch of the first agrarian judicial district in Tunja and its five circuit courts.
The Fund has strengthened its support for Territorially Focused Development Programs (PDET) process in Catatumbo by finalizing a major rural value chain initiative and accelerating 340 local development projects. It helped formalize two regional cooperatives, delivered technical training, equipment, and set up revolving commercialization funds, leading to new market alliances. Work with indigenous communities focused on aligning PDET initiatives with their governance and life plans. A national guide will ensure these approaches are replicated in other PDET regions.
- Action Against Mines: The contribution has contributed to several results regarding Comprehensive Action Against Anti-Personnel Mines. the Fund's support to mine action focused on strengthening national capacities for mine risk education and humanitarian demining. With technical support from SENA and OCCP, 30 organizations began an accreditation process to carry out Mine Risk Education (ERAE), and 166 individuals across 16 departments were certified. Moreover, the Fund contributed to multiple community development initiatives, including school improvements, solar panel installations, and women-led projects. Finally, Humanicemos DH submitted a reparative procedure proposal (TOAR) to JEP, seeking recognition of mine action as a part of Colombia's transitional justice process.
- Victims and Transitional Justice: UNMPTF strengthened the 16 Peace Seats (Curules de Paz) by training social leaders and advising civil society organizations on legislative matters, which enables the construction and presentation of 8 draft laws in Congress and 75 legislative proposals focused on rural and victims' rights. The fund has organized spaces for dialogue for victims' organizations and has gathered data from 11 800 people across the country to inform implementation, monitoring and decision-making about the relevance and satisfaction with the implementation of Peace Agreement. The fund has provided funding to support the work of the Search Unit (UBPD) that contributed to giving psychosocial support to individuals, 925 new disappearance cases have been documented and new burial sites been identified and registered. 10 of the 11 macro-cases that are being investigated by the Special Jurisdiction for Peace had received technical support to advance in the resolution of the most relevant human rights violations.
- Reincorporation: The fund has supported 120 collective and 1,238 individual productive projects, benefiting 9,846 former FARC-EP members. The support has enabled income generation and deeper socio-economic integration through the strengthening of associative capacities, technical assistance and skill training. Environmentally sustainable practices were promoted across all projects and contributed to the development of a national Economic Sustainability Strategy, officially adopted by the Colombian government through Resolution 1369 of 2024. Moreover, UN MPTF had contributed to improving trust between the state and the FARC peace signatories through technical assistance and the accompaniment of the United Nations system.
- Communication: Ten lead organizations and 39 partners across 13 departments strengthened local communication capacities, helping to raise awareness of the progress and challenges of the PDET and the peace process through different media channels. Additionally, the Fund has supported the Technical Secretariat of the international verification component of CSIVI who published two reports that highlights the progress in rural reform, territorial transformation, and the inclusion of 80 new indicators in the Implementation Framework Plan (PMI). The Secretariat also developed an information repository (infoverificapaz.org.co). The support from the Fund was instrumental in updating the PMI and proposing an extension of the peace implementation period to 2038.
- Peacebuilding beyond the 2016 Agreement: The Fund supported the Colombian government's expanded peace agenda by strengthening the role of the Catholic Church in the ceasefire monitoring mechanism with the ELN, formalized by Decree 104 of 2024. The Church conducted preparatory activities, including regional and national meetings, and signed 21 agreements to implement localized peacebuilding and pedagogical efforts. The initiative produced key reports and diagnostics on conflict-related impacts and helped create safe spaces that fostered social cohesion and increased community participation in peace processes.
The Fund is one of the most important mechanisms for dialogue between donors and the government, facilitating the implementation of the peace agreement, aligning peace policies, and identifying the most significant gaps and bottlenecks in the implementation of the agreement's measures. The steering and strategic committees are important platforms for conveying key messages from donors to institutional leaders and for discussing the national government's priorities.
The Fund is also relevant because its approach has promoted innovation and the catalytic use of resources to increase the impact of funded projects. An example of this is the Fund's leveraged resources, which have increased every year since its inception. To date, the Fund has leveraged approximately USD 267 million. This sum includes resources from the private sector, public investments, philanthropy, and contributions from UN agencies.
The Fund is prioritizing joint efforts with the private sector, two calls for proposals for blended finance initiatives have been made, one in 2019 and the other in 2023. The most recent call for proposals began implementing the initiatives in August 2024 with seven different private sector entities, achieving a leverage ratio of 1:4. These initiatives implement five innovative financing mechanisms, such as guaranteeing resources for 'multi-activity' parametric insurance policies, providing interest rate subsidies, and establishing first loss or risk funds. These alliances contribute to mobilising the private sector to invest in conflict-affected areas, reducing their risks with the support of the Fund.
